body:
The basic source of nuclear electricity

In a nuclear power station, energy released through controlled nuclear fission is converted into heat and then used to generate electricity. The process differs fundamentally from burning coal, petroleum or natural gas.

In a coal-fired power station, combustion releases heat and produces carbon dioxide as a direct consequence of burning carbon-containing fuel. In a nuclear power station, the fission process produces heat without burning fossil fuel. Consequently, nuclear electricity generation has very low direct operational carbon dioxide emissions.

This does not mean that nuclear electricity has absolutely no environmental impact. Mining, fuel preparation, construction, maintenance, waste management and decommissioning can produce greenhouse-gas emissions. These are considered when assessing life-cycle emissions, which cover the wider activities needed to produce electricity over the facility's life.

Low-carbon does not mean renewable

A low-carbon energy source produces relatively little greenhouse-gas emissions per unit of energy when assessed over the relevant life cycle. A renewable energy source is replenished naturally on a human timescale.

Nuclear electricity is generally classified as low-carbon but non-renewable, because conventional nuclear power depends on finite nuclear-fuel resources. Solar and wind energy are renewable and also have low life-cycle greenhouse-gas emissions. Coal is non-renewable and has high emissions from combustion.

How nuclear power contributes to reliable electricity supply

Electricity demand continues during the night, on cloudy days and during periods of low wind. Nuclear power stations can generate substantial electricity over extended periods, provided the station is operating normally and sufficient fuel and cooling resources are available.

This characteristic makes nuclear generation a source of firm, low-emission electricity. It can support the electricity system when the output of weather-dependent renewable sources is limited. The International Energy Agency identifies nuclear power as a dispatchable, low-emission source that can complement renewable electricity.

However, the word reliable does not mean that a nuclear reactor can never shut down. Planned maintenance, refuelling and unexpected outages affect actual generation. A power system must maintain a suitable combination of generation sources, reserves, transmission and operational arrangements to meet demand.

Firm supply and flexible supply are not identical

Firm supply refers to electricity that is available with a high degree of dependability under the relevant operating conditions. Flexibility refers to the ability to change output when demand or other sources of generation change.

Nuclear stations may operate for long periods at high output, and some can adjust their generation. Nevertheless, their practical flexibility depends on the plant and operating circumstances. It is incorrect to assume that all nuclear stations can instantly replace any shortfall in the electricity system.

Nuclear fuel resources in India

Uranium is an important fuel resource for conventional nuclear power. Indian uranium occurrences include areas of Jharkhand, particularly the Singhbhum region, and parts of Rajasthan.

Thorium is found notably in monazite-bearing coastal sands, including areas along the coasts of Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Thorium is important to India's long-term nuclear-energy strategy, but it is not interchangeable with uranium in ordinary reactor operation. Thorium requires an appropriate nuclear fuel-cycle process before it can support sustained energy generation: fertile thorium-232 is converted into fissile uranium-233 through neutron absorption followed by radioactive decay.

The existence of a mineral deposit does not, by itself, establish that the material is currently being used commercially in all nuclear power stations. Resource availability, technology, safety arrangements and economic feasibility remain relevant.

Three distinct questions: Is the energy source low-carbon? Is its resource renewable? Can it provide electricity dependably when needed? A source can satisfy one of these conditions without satisfying all 3.

Prelims focus

  • Nuclear fission generates heat without fossil-fuel combustion.
  • Nuclear electricity is low-carbon but generally non-renewable.
  • Life-cycle emissions include activities beyond electricity generation itself.
  • Firm electricity supply is not the same as unlimited operational flexibility.
  • Important Indian uranium occurrences include Jharkhand and Rajasthan.
  • Trap: Thorium-bearing monazite sands do not mean that thorium can be used directly in every conventional nuclear reactor.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 8 Geography, Resources and Development, chapter Mineral and Power Resources, printed pp. 34-35; NCERT, Class 12 Geography, India: People and Economy, chapter Mineral and Energy Resources, printed pp. 80-82; International Energy Agency, The Path to a New Era for Nuclear Energy, Executive Summary, 16 January 2025; consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Why Nuclear Electricity Is Considered Low-Carbon and Reliable

body:
Why nuclear power remains a subject of debate

The debate over nuclear electricity is not simply a disagreement about whether nuclear energy can produce power. Its ability to generate large quantities of low-carbon electricity is established. The debate concerns whether, where and how nuclear power should be expanded after considering its costs, construction time, radioactive waste, accident risks, security requirements and effects on communities.

Different countries may reach different policy decisions because their electricity demand, financial resources, existing power systems, regulatory capacity and public priorities differ.

High initial cost and construction time

A nuclear power station generally requires substantial expenditure before it begins supplying electricity. Expenditure may involve site preparation, construction, specialised equipment, safety systems, regulatory compliance and supporting infrastructure.

Large nuclear projects can have long planning and construction periods. Delays may increase costs because money remains invested before electricity sales begin. The International Energy Agency identifies capital intensity, construction lead times, technical complexity and cost overruns as important financing challenges for new nuclear projects.

Once operating, a nuclear station can produce electricity over an extended period, and its fuel costs are generally a smaller part of its overall costs than construction and financing. Whether nuclear electricity is economical therefore depends on the actual project costs, financing conditions, operating performance and plant lifetime.

It is misleading to describe nuclear power as either always cheap or always expensive. Costs vary between projects and countries. Extending the life of a safe existing plant is also a different economic decision from constructing a completely new station.

Radioactive waste and its long-term management

Nuclear electricity produces radioactive waste and spent nuclear fuel; India treats spent fuel as a resource for reprocessing. Spent fuel remains radioactive and can continue producing heat after removal from a reactor. It therefore requires controlled handling, shielding and cooling.

Spent fuel is commonly stored initially in specially designed water-filled pools. It may subsequently be transferred to an appropriate wet or dry storage facility. Countries also consider longer-term management options, including reprocessing and final disposal, according to their policies and technical arrangements.

Storage and disposal are different concepts. Storage involves keeping radioactive material in a controlled facility while retaining the possibility of retrieval. Disposal is intended to provide long-term isolation without routine retrieval. Deep geological disposal is an important long-term option for suitable high-level radioactive waste, but implementation depends on technical, regulatory and social conditions.

Reprocessing may recover useful nuclear material from spent fuel. However, it does not eliminate all radioactive waste or the need for safe waste management. It can also introduce additional safeguards and security considerations.

Accident prevention and nuclear safety

The possible consequences of a severe nuclear accident make safety regulation particularly important. The Chernobyl accident in 1986 and the Fukushima Daiichi accident in 2011 illustrate why plant safety, emergency preparedness, regulatory supervision and lessons from accidents remain significant.

Safety measures seek to prevent accidents, control radiation exposure and reduce consequences if an accident occurs. The relevant responsibilities continue throughout the life of a facility, including operation, waste management and eventual decommissioning.

A low probability of a severe accident does not mean that the consequences can be ignored. Equally, the existence of accident risk does not establish that every nuclear installation is equally dangerous. Assessment must consider the specific facility, its safety provisions, surrounding conditions and regulatory oversight.

Proliferation and security concerns

Civil nuclear cooperation can involve sensitive material and technology. Safeguards and export controls aim to prevent peaceful nuclear activities from contributing to nuclear weapons programmes. Physical protection and nuclear security measures address theft, sabotage and other deliberate threats.

These concerns are not identical to ordinary plant safety. A nuclear facility can require strong safeguards and security arrangements even when its daily operation meets applicable safety requirements.

Public acceptance and community concerns

Communities near a proposed nuclear installation may be concerned about safety, land use, local livelihoods, environmental impacts, water resources, emergency arrangements and the handling of radioactive waste.

Public acceptance is influenced not only by technical assessments but also by the credibility of information, transparent decision-making, opportunities for participation and confidence in institutions responsible for safety.

Public opposition cannot automatically be dismissed as ignorance, just as public support does not remove the need for rigorous regulation. An informed decision requires accurate information about both benefits and risks.

The Gujarat connection: Kakrapar Atomic Power Station

The Kakrapar Atomic Power Station, near Surat in Gujarat, provides a concrete example of nuclear electricity generation within the state.

According to the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited's operating-performance information for FY 2026-27, with generation data covering April-August 2026, Kakrapar has 4 listed pressurised heavy water reactor units:

  • Units 1 and 2: 220 MWe each.
  • Units 3 and 4: 700 MWe each.
  • Combined installed electrical capacity: 1,840 MWe.

NPCIL gives 30 June 2023 as the commercial-operation date of Unit 3 and 31 March 2024 for Unit 4. These are historical commissioning facts, not forecasts.

The unit MWe means megawatts of electrical capacity. The installed capacity of 1,840 MWe is not the same as electricity actually generated over a year. Actual generation depends on operating hours, maintenance and plant performance.

Kakrapar illustrates the contribution of nuclear power to Gujarat's electricity supply. It also shows why nuclear development must be considered together with safety regulation, waste management and public confidence rather than only installed capacity.

Bringing the international and energy questions together

International nuclear governance and the nuclear-energy debate address connected but different questions. The NPT sets treaty commitments on non-proliferation, peaceful uses and disarmament. The IAEA verifies safeguards commitments and supports safety cooperation. The NSG coordinates nuclear export-control guidelines. The CTBT seeks to prohibit nuclear explosions but has not yet entered into force. National civil-liability law identifies responsibility for compensation following nuclear damage.

These arrangements do not by themselves determine whether a country should build a nuclear power station. Such a decision must also examine low-carbon electricity needs, reliability, construction time, costs, radioactive waste, accident prevention, proliferation risks and public acceptance.

Balanced conclusion: Nuclear power can provide reliable, low-carbon electricity, but its benefits must be evaluated alongside long construction periods, major initial expenditure, waste obligations, safety and security requirements, and public concerns. No single advantage or disadvantage determines the entire energy-policy decision.

Prelims focus

  • Nuclear projects may involve high initial investment and long construction periods.
  • Spent nuclear fuel requires controlled cooling and radioactive-material management.
  • Storage and final disposal of radioactive waste are different processes.
  • Kakrapar Atomic Power Station is in Gujarat near Surat.
  • Kakrapar Units 3 and 4 have installed capacities of 700 MWe each.
  • Trap: Installed electrical capacity in MWe does not represent the electricity generated over a year.

[Sources: International Energy Agency, The Path to a New Era for Nuclear Energy, chapter Financing Nuclear Projects, 16 January 2025; IAEA, Storage of Spent Nuclear Fuel, sections on storage safety and spent-fuel storage arrangements; IAEA, Nuclear Safety and Security Frequently Asked Questions, entry dated 4 September 2023; Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited, Kakrapar Atomic Power Station, Operating Performance and Generation Statistics, FY 2026-27, April-August 2026 data; NCERT, Class 12 Geography, India: People and Economy, chapter Mineral and Energy Resources, printed pp. 80-82; consulted 16 November 2026.]
